title: Trump promises $5,000 dividend to every U.S. adult if Republicans hold midterms
dek: Donald Trump promised to distribute $5,000 to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The proposal would cost approximately $1.2 trillion, funded in part by tariff revenue according to Vice President JD Vance. Economists and experts question the plan's feasibility, budget math, and how it would navigate congressional approval.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Trump announced a $1.2 trillion plan to pay every U.S. adult $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, contingent on congressional approval and tariff revenue funding.
bottom_line: Congressional approval would be required for any dividend payments to be made. The cost, funding mechanism, and beneficiary definition remain unspecified, and Trump's prior similar promises were not fulfilled.
body: Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult U.S. citizen a $5,000 dividend if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, according to PBS NewsHour reporting. Trump made the pledge during a speech at the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas and said the payment would be called the "Trump dividend."

The U.S. Census Bureau estimates there are about 245 million U.S. citizen adults. Giving each of them a $5,000 check would cost approximately $1.2 trillion. Trump said the rationale behind the proposal was the country's "tremendous economic success." He compared the dividend check to successful companies distributing cash to shareholders and pointed to his administration's decision to give members of the military $1,776 checks in December.

Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that some of the money would come from tariff revenue. However, Vance separately told Fox News the money would be for "the American middle class" and for "American workers," a description narrower than Trump's stated commitment to "every adult citizen in the United States of America," which could exclude U.S. citizens living abroad. The Association of Americans Resident Overseas estimated 5.5 million Americans lived abroad in 2024, a number that includes children.

The proposal immediately raised concerns about feasibility and cost. Any proposal involving sending checks to Americans requires congressional approval. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, wrote on X that he would introduce a bill to "get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election."

Economists questioned whether tariff revenue could cover the expense. The Tax Foundation reported that Trump's tariffs would generate about $158 billion in revenue in 2025 and $208 billion in 2026. Erica York, senior economist at the Tax Foundation, wrote that the cost of the $5,000 checks would spend "almost all the revenue that the new tariffs are projected to bring in over a decade." York stated the pledge is "Not gonna happen." Spending $1.2 trillion to send checks to Americans would affect the national debt and economic inflation, which lawmakers might oppose, per PBS reporting.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund and a Harvard University economics professor, said: "The U.S. is already running an unsustainable deficit, this would only blow up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years."

The Supreme Court struck down most of Trump's earlier tariffs in February 2026. After the ruling, Trump imposed a global 10 percent tariff. Trump promised to give Americans $2,000 tariff dividend checks in November 2024, according to PBS; those checks never went out. The Tax Foundation published a report saying U.S. tariff revenue would not be able to cover the $280 to $607 billion cost of those promised $2,000 dividend checks.

Election law experts said the promise itself is likely legal. Rick Hasen, an election law professor at UCLA, wrote that Trump would have a strong First Amendment defense for promising a financial incentive during an election and that the checks "are constitutionally protected," though he questioned Trump's ability to get congressional approval. Hasen cited the 1982 U.S. Supreme Court case Brown v. Hartlage, in which the court ruled that a Kentucky county candidate did not violate an anticorruption law when promising to lower commissioner's salaries. Richard Painter, a government ethics expert and corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, agreed that candidates are allowed to make campaign promises involving taxes, spending, and social programs. Painter compared Trump's plan to Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern's promise in 1972 to give every American $1,000 a year if elected. McGovern lost to incumbent President Richard Nixon, and Painter said voters saw through the promise and understood it would cause inflation.

The White House did not directly respond to PBS News' question about how tariff revenue would cover the cost. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told PBS: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats' record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage."

In February 2025, Trump and billionaire Elon Musk endorsed a proposal to give Americans "DOGE dividend checks" from savings secured by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which Musk briefly oversaw. Musk's aim was to save $2 trillion in spending cuts, which would translate to checks of about $5,000. The DOGE dividend checks did not materialize, and DOGE did not save $2 trillion via spending cuts. DOGE's "Wall of Receipts" claimed $110 billion in savings, but a government watchdog said in an August 2026 report that the DOGE savings figure was made up of estimates that were incorrect or lacked supporting evidence.
consolidated: This story was updated in place with a better-sourced account of the same event, carrying 5 sources against the original 6. The earlier version was headlined “Trump promises $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win midterms”. The URL and publication time are unchanged.
